why.A: A temperature optimum does not rule out other factors.

context: According to Scientist 1, the timing of the extinctions corresponds most closely to:

choices.text: a comet fragmented over the ice sheet.
the Northern Hemisphere cooled abruptly about 12,900 years ago.

why.A: Only Scientist 2 makes this claim.
why.B: Correct — the shared premise is stated in the introduction and accepted by both.
why.C: Scientist 1 makes circulation central.
why.D: Both describe an abrupt onset.

context: Which finding would most weaken Scientist 1’s hypothesis?

choices.text: Evidence that the Southern Hemisphere cooled just as much as the Northern.
Evidence of elevated platinum in sediments.
Evidence that the cooling began within decades.
Evidence that a glacial lake existed in North America.

why.A: Correct — Scientist 1’s mechanism predicts an asymmetric, northern-focused cooling, so symmetric cooling contradicts it directly.
why.B: This supports Scientist 2 without disproving a circulation change.
why.C: Scientist 2 emphasizes abruptness, but a sudden lake drainage could also act quickly.
why.D: This supports Scientist 1.

context: Scientist 1 cites St. Lawrence sediment cores in order to:

choices.text: provide physical evidence that a large discharge occurred at the right time.

why.A: Scientist 1 rejects the impact explanation.
why.B: Correct — the cores document the drainage event the hypothesis requires.
why.C: The cores are from North America, not the Southern Hemisphere.
why.D: Wildfires belong to Scientist 2’s account.

context: Scientist 2 argues the abruptness of the onset favors an impact because:

choices.text: a sudden catastrophic trigger better matches a change occurring within decades.

why.A: Scientist 2 says a catastrophic trigger fits better, not that ocean change is always slow.
why.B: Correct — this is the stated reasoning about timescale.
why.C: No such universal claim is made.
why.D: Scientist 2 relies on decadal resolution rather than disputing it.

context: If the impact materials were later shown to occur at many different dates rather than only at 12,900 years ago, this would:

choices.text: weaken Scientist 2’s hypothesis by removing the link to this specific event.
have no bearing on either hypothesis.

why.A: The argument depends on the materials being confined to that layer.
why.B: Correct — if the markers are common across many dates, they no longer single out the Younger Dryas onset.
why.C: Scientist 1’s meltwater mechanism is untouched by this finding.
why.D: It bears directly on Scientist 2’s central evidence.

context: The two hypotheses differ mainly in:

choices.text: whether the cooling occurred at all.
the mechanism that initiated the cooling.

why.A: Both accept the cooling as established.
why.B: Correct — meltwater disrupting circulation versus an impact triggering wildfires and soot.
why.C: Neither disputes the roughly 1,200-year duration.
why.D: Only Scientist 1 raises hemispheric asymmetry, and Scientist 2 does not contest it.
